### PROCESS 77.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
Take Tartarized Tartar <note>potassium tartrate</note>, properly prepared according to Process 75 and dried, and reduce it to a fine powder. In a tall chemical vial, pour over it the purest <term>Alkohol</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss> of wine until it exceeds the powder by four inches. Then, with the vial closed only by paper, let them boil together as gently as possible in our wooden furnace for the space of a <term>nycthemeron</term> <gloss>a full day and night</gloss>. The spirit will be seen floating on top with a golden color, an aromatic odor, and a penetrating, warm taste. If this is repeated with fresh alcohol in the same manner, a white salt will eventually be left at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened over a gentle fire until a tenth part remains concentrated at the bottom.

#### USES.
This serves to demonstrate the part in that salt which is soluble in alcohol. The prepared tincture itself is aromatic, warming, and consolidates ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, which is simpler than before, shows that salts can be whitened by drawing out the tincture with the help of alcohol.

### PROCESS 78.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
Take Regenerated Tartar <note>potassium acetate</note>, previously prepared as cleanly as possible and, as far as can be done, most safely. In a tall chemical glass vial, pour six times the amount of the purest alcohol. Cook this as carefully as possible over a gentle fire in our wooden furnace. The substances will combine with one another, and they will become a single, uniformly composed thing once the dregs have settled to the bottom. After they have settled accurately through rest, let the clear, supernatant liquor flow out by carefully tilting the vessel. If any undissolved saline matter remains, it can be dissolved with the same caution by applying fresh alcohol and separated from the dreggy part. Then, the prepared liquors should be concentrated to half their volume by distilling with a very gentle fire; this will produce the Tincture of this Salt.

#### USES.
In this experiment, you see united into one substance the alkali, the oily acid, and the oily spirits of vegetables. From this come the most active principles of plants, freed from inert earth; yet at the same time they are safe enough, possessing no further dangerous acrimony. These things, thus united, seem to constitute even the "Small Elixir of the Wise" <note>original: "Elixir parvum Sapientum"</note>, which the Masters of the Ancient Art recommended for preserving and restoring health. It completely dispels almost all obstacles; it <column-break/> penetrates through the vessels with a pleasant stimulus to incite life, so that it heals through <term>diaphoresis</term> <gloss>perspiration</gloss>. In chemical matters, it also provides a most effective solvent by which substances are reduced to their smallest, active parts, with their <term>seminal virtue</term> <gloss>essential power</gloss> left intact, so that they can be admitted into the innermost parts of the body to restrain and subdue all rebellious conditions. Nor is it less praised for the beauty of its effects which it provides for external bodily evils, such as wounds, ulcers, and tumors. Furthermore, this most wholesome remedy should not be denied to the poor out of ambition; for it can be prepared instantly by mixing <term>Cineres clavellatos</term> <gloss>potash or pearl ash</gloss> with fifteen times the amount of the sharpest vinegar, then straining and thickening it. Thus, without the expense of labor or price, a suitable remedy can be prepared and used. This was known to the ancients in Rome. Pliny, Book 23, in the Preface: "The ash of vine-twigs sprinkled with vinegar is drunk for defects of the spleen."

### PROCESS 79.
**Harvey’s Tincture of Salt of Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
I take the very black alkaline salt which remained in the glass retort after all the volatile matter was driven out from Tartar by distillation using the highest heat of a sand-bath, according to Process 55. This salt is quickly crushed into a powder in a warm iron mortar with a warm pestle and placed into a tall glass vial. I pour over it the best common spirits of wine so that it floats four fingers deep. I cook it over a gentle fire in this tall vial, in our wooden furnace, for twenty hours. A thin, black liquor will be obtained, with a bitter, aromatic, and lye-like taste. Let it be poured off in its pure state. Thus, it can be kept unharmed in a closed vessel for its required uses under its own title.

#### USES.
Common spirit of wine, consisting of water, acid, and alcohol united together, when boiled with the alkali of Tartar that is still oily, makes a milder and safer lye. This is because the alkali is tempered by the acid, oil, and alcohol; from this arises a type of medicament and solvent that is not ignoble. In chemistry, when cooked or digested with vegetable substances, it performs well by beautifully dissolving simples. In surgery, it is a most noble remedy for purifying, cleansing, drying, and consolidating ulcers that are moist and purulent, putrid, foul, virulent, or malignant, whether they are fistulous, winding, or spreading like a burrow; it is also used to consume those things which grow out with excessive luxury <note>excessive granulation tissue or proud flesh</note>, especially if it is mixed skillfully with a little oil.
